t: Upholding rule by institutions and rule by Party regulations in governing the Party
zh: 坚持制度治党、依规治党
paras: This commentary, originally published in the People's Daily, sets out what it means to govern the Party through institutions (zhidu zhi dang) and through Party regulations (yi gui zhi dang), why this matters and how to do it. Li Binxiong argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has treated this approach as the long-term and fundamental basis of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. In Li's account it is an important component of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building.

The piece is organised in three parts, each built around quotations from the Selected Writings of Xi Jinping on Party Building. The first part defines the concept and its features. The second explains its significance for the Party's leadership, for Party building and for long-term rule. The third sets out practical requirements.

In the first part, Li defines institution-based governance as the Party using rules and systems to guide, regulate and safeguard its governance, and regulation-based governance as doing the same through intra-Party regulations. Li cites Xi's view that regulations and institutions are fundamental, comprehensive, stable and long-term, and presents four requirements: rules to rely on, rules that must be followed, rules strictly enforced, and violations investigated. In the second part, Li argues that this approach turns the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds into institutional norms, secures the Party's comprehensive leadership and helps the Party escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. It is also said to support the Party's self-purification and to align state law with Party regulation.

On practice, Li calls for three things. First, a sound institutional system built on systemic, dialectical and bottom-line thinking, balancing strict management with care for officials and keeping rules up to date. Second, stronger institutional awareness and enforcement, so that rules are not treated as soft advocacy but as binding constraints. Third, a clear responsibility system with enforcement duties and strict accountability, including investigation of leaders where enforcement fails. Read the original if you want a compact, official-style statement of how the Party's regulatory approach to self-governance is justified and what its stated implementation priorities are.
quoteEn: Upholding rule by institutions and by Party regulations is not a soft advocacy that is "important in word but secondary in deed", but a rigid constraint pursued with the resolve to leave marks on iron and footprints on stone.
quoteZh: 坚持制度治党、依规治党，不是“说起来重要、做起来次要”的柔性倡导，而是抓铁有痕、踏石留印的刚性约束。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's drive since 2012 to tighten discipline, combat corruption and strengthen internal oversight.

t: Persist in advancing the three-pronged approach of not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt as an integrated whole
zh: 坚持一体推进不敢腐不能腐不想腐
paras: This commentary, published in the People's Daily, takes up the Party's principle of advancing, as one whole, the aims of making officials not dare to be corrupt, not able to be corrupt and not want to be corrupt. Song Xueqin argues that the principle is both a basic guideline of the anti-corruption struggle and an important strategy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. In the author's account it is an original theoretical result of Xi Jinping's leadership of that struggle, and it has shifted corruption governance from treating symptoms to addressing symptoms and root causes together.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the principle's standing and its theoretical underpinnings. The second explains how the three components work in practice. The third assesses the current situation and proposes measures. Song draws on passages from the second volume of Selected Works of Xi Jinping on Party Building, and on Party figures such as the 2025 number of people who turned themselves in.

Song describes the three components as interdependent: not daring is the precondition, not being able is the key, and not wanting is the foundation. Deterrence through strict punishment clears existing corruption and curbs new cases. Institutional constraints, by closing gaps in how power is allocated, exercised and supervised, move governance from passive punishment to active prevention. Ideological education and a culture of integrity are said to produce voluntary self-discipline, which Song calls the most durable barrier. The author contends that fragmented or one-dimensional governance can no longer meet current needs. In the author's view the approach also differs from Western parties' reliance on external checks and purely legal restraint.

Song states that the anti-corruption struggle has won an overwhelming victory that has been consolidated, but remains severe and complex, with old corruption not yet cleared and new cases emerging. The author calls for stronger centralised Party leadership and responsibility systems, close attention to new and hidden forms of corruption, and use of the "four forms" of supervision and discipline. Further proposals include tighter rules on power and joined-up supervision, harsher punishment of bribe-giving, and tailored integrity education. Song concludes that these efforts will provide political assurance for building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale and policy agenda behind the three "nots" formula in Party anti-corruption discourse.
quoteEn: "Not daring" is the precondition, "not being able" is the key and "not wanting" is the foundation; the three are interdependent, mutually reinforcing and dialectically unified.
quoteZh: “不敢”是前提、“不能”是关键、“不想”是根本，三者相互依存、相互促进、辩证统一。

A graded approach to discipline: criticism and light sanctions as the norm, then heavier sanctions, then major adjustments, and finally investigation of serious violations.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official long-term national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, central to Xi Jinping-era political discourse.

t: The dialectical implications of the Communist Party of China's self-reform
zh: 中国共产党自我革命的辩证意蕴
paras: He Changyu takes up the Party's self-reform, which Xi Jinping describes as the Party's most distinctive trait and greatest strength. Earlier scholarship has located its philosophical basis in the mass view of history. The article argues that it can also be read through the logic of materialist dialectics, and that self-reform is an application and development of dialectics in Party building.

The article is organised around three questions. The first asks what self-reform is, using dialectical logic. The second asks why the Party must undertake it, through several dialectical relationships. The third asks how it should be advanced, through paired practical principles. The author draws on Marx, Engels, Hegel, Mao Zedong and Xi, and repeatedly contrasts the case of the Soviet Communist Party's collapse.

On definition, He holds that self-reform is a substantive, object-oriented revolution aimed at specific problems: wavering ideals, disregard of political discipline, lack of competence, and poor conduct. It is also a revolution of negation of the negation that ends in self-affirmation, which the author distinguishes from the historical nihilism said to have destroyed the Soviet party. It is also a long-term undertaking that is always under way. On necessity, He argues that it follows from the unity of Party spirit and the people's character, from long-term rule combined with consensus among the people, which is needed to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall, and from the unity of upholding fundamental principles and innovation. On method, He proposes combining the main thrust with the strategic goal (the 'unique challenges of a large party'), intra-Party supervision with supervision by the people, organisational drive with individual initiative, and strict management with caring support.

He concludes that self-reform is the Party's 'second answer' to the historical cycle, building on the 'first answer' of people's supervision, which it does not replace. In He's account, internal causes work through external conditions, so the two forms of supervision must reinforce each other. The article's practical proposals include clear assignment of responsibility, higher standards for senior cadres, heart-to-heart talks and early correction of minor errors. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how the Party's anti-corruption and self-discipline agenda is justified in terms of dialectical method.
quoteEn: The Party's self-reform is not a merely formal change.
quoteZh: 党的自我革命不是单纯形式化的变革。

glossary.explanation: A term prominent in Xi Jinping-era Party discourse for the Party's continuous internal purification, improvement, renewal and enhancement, including anti-corruption and discipline work. It is presented as the answer to how a long-ruling party avoids degeneration.

glossary.en: historical cycle of rise and fall
glossary.explanation: The pattern, discussed by Huang Yanpei and Mao Zedong in 1945, in which regimes flourish and then abruptly decline. Party texts present escaping it as the aim of long-term rule.

glossary.en: unique challenges of a large party
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formulation, summarised as 'six how-to-always' problems, of difficulties specific to a very large ruling party, such as unity of will, governing capacity and a clean political environment.

t: How the Red Army built discipline on the Long March
zh: 长征路上红军如何开展纪律建设
paras: Marking the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victory in 2026, Liu Jie asks how the Red Army kept itself together under extreme pressure. The author argues that strong discipline-building was an important guarantee of victory, citing Zhu De's remark that on the Long March "we lived by discipline". Observing discipline is presented as a core part of the Long March spirit and a key to reading the Long March "miracle" and passing on the Party's red genes.

The article is a short commentary built around three practices drawn from the Party Central Committee and Central Military Commission record: discipline education, combining work style with discipline in mass work, and strict supervision and enforcement. Liu draws on Red Army orders, the newspaper Red Star, proclamations issued in Yi and Hui areas, and individual disciplinary cases. It closes by linking these experiences to present-day Party governance.

On education, Liu describes a layered system: written directives such as the 1934 political-work instruction, case-based articles in Red Star, and memorable slogans like the "Eight Points for Attention on entering Zunyi" for a largely illiterate army. On mass work, the author argues that publicly announcing ethnic and discipline policies before entering Yi and Hui areas gave local people a concrete standard by which to monitor the army. Liu says that the army's conduct then won trust, with Yi and Hui youths joining it. On enforcement, the author points to inspection teams at corps, division and regiment level, and to public trials and executions of personnel for extortion, embezzlement and dereliction of duty.

Liu concludes that firm Party spirit, good Party conduct and strict Party discipline explain how the Party has endured, and that each generation has its own Long March. The author calls for sustained full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, citing Xi Jinping on strict supervision as a weapon of the Party's self-reform. Liu also urges handling violations early and in small matters, and neither wronging the innocent nor excusing the guilty. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of Long March discipline cases and how they are used to support current Party-discipline messaging.
quoteEn: Observing discipline is both an important part of the Long March spirit and the key to understanding the Long March miracle and passing on the red genes.
quoteZh: 严守纪律既是长征精神的重要内涵，也是我们解读长征奇迹、传承红色基因的关键所在。

t: A historical examination of the building of daily-life discipline in the Red Army during the Long March
zh: 长征途中红军生活纪律建设的历史考察
paras: Li and Sun take up a topic they say has received little attention. Scholarship on the Long March has concentrated on policy, key meetings, the Long March spirit, leaders and military command, while the daily-life discipline that governed Red Army conduct has been neglected. Drawing on published archives and memoirs, they argue that the Party Centre steadily built up this discipline in response to changing circumstances, and that it was an important guarantee of the march's success.

The article has three main parts. The first explains why daily-life discipline arose: the pressure of Nationalist encirclement and harsh terrain, the need to forge a reliable force, the need to win popular support, and the need to hold the army together. The second describes how the discipline was constructed, as an integrated system of regulation, propaganda, leadership example, enforcement and supervision. The third assesses results. A short conclusion draws lessons for the present.

The authors' central claim is that daily-life discipline was not an external restraint but became an internalised habit and value, moving from "being made to obey" to "wanting to obey". They point to directives of the General Political Department on ethnic minorities and grain purchases, to the Red Star newspaper, songs and slogans, to Mao Zedong's stretcher and Peng Dehuai's mule as examples set by leaders, and to inspection teams, local work departments, Communist Youth League members and complaints from local people as a multi-layered supervisory system. They also cite Zhang Guotao's challenge to the Centre as a case of indiscipline that failed.

The authors report four results: the trust of local people, who supplied food and information; an upright style within the army; large-scale recruitment, which they put at about 20,000 for the First Front Army alone; and stronger combat capacity, illustrated by the 34th Division at the Xiang River. They conclude that strict discipline is the basis of victory and of a strong army. They call for carrying this "red gene" into military education, in support of building a world-class army and of national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the Red Army's everyday conduct rules were framed, propagated and enforced during the Long March, as presented in current Chinese military-history scholarship.
quoteEn: Daily-life discipline was not an external constraint imposed on the Red Army, but a necessary choice the Red Army made, amid the currents of history, in order to survive and develop.
quoteZh: 生活纪律并非强加给红军的外在束缚，而是红军在历史洪流中为了生存发展而作出的必然选择

glossary.explanation: The official Party formulation of China's own path of modernization, used since the early 2020s as the framework for national development goals.
The Red Army's main newspaper during the Long March, used to publish discipline rules, model examples and warnings about violations.

t: Using digital empowerment to promote high-quality development of discipline inspection and supervision work
zh: 以数字赋能推动纪检监察工作高质量发展
paras: Gong Bihan takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, to grasp new trends in corruption and innovate methods. The commentary argues that integrating big data and artificial intelligence into discipline inspection and supervision is more than a tool upgrade. In Gong's view it is a revolution in supervising public power and a reshaping of the governance paradigm.

The piece examines four areas: the fundamental guiding principle, the value orientation, the mechanism through which digital tools work, and the practical path of implementation. It is a short newspaper commentary built as four numbered sections.

Gong holds that digital systems must stay under the Party's centralised, unified leadership and serve full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, with its political requirements built into the algorithms. The value orientation is a people-centred approach, with data monitoring of livelihood areas such as education, healthcare, pensions and rural revitalisation, and online platforms that lower barriers to public participation. On mechanism, Gong describes anti-corruption penetration deepening from static structure to dynamic process to underlying logic. Knowledge graphs would expose institutional loopholes, risk thresholds would flag procedural anomalies, and machine learning on past cases would predict risks, shifting supervision from punishing existing problems to preventing future ones.

Gong proposes four measures: break down data silos through unified standards and lawful data sharing; build intelligent analytical models to detect abnormal fund flows and hidden interest-transfer chains; embed data analysis in the whole case workflow, moving from manual checks to human–machine collaboration; and establish rules on data security, algorithm audits and compliance to guard against leaks, algorithmic bias and abuse of power. Gong presents this as converting institutional strengths into governance effectiveness and consolidating the Party's anti-corruption gains. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-affiliated researchers frame digital technology in anti-corruption supervision.
quoteEn: Piling up data produces no value; only correlation analysis can reveal the truth.
quoteZh: 数据堆砌不产生价值，关联分析才能揭示真相。

t: Drawing on traditional Chinese thought on clean governance
zh: 汲取中华传统廉政思想养分
paras: This newspaper commentary, published in Henan Daily in 2026, asks how the clean-governance thought of China's traditional culture can feed the building of a culture of integrity in the new era. Sun argues that five strands of that thought, though limited by their time, still offer a systematic resource. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping on learning from the history of anti-corruption work.

The article takes five strands in turn, each tied to one representative figure and one dimension: public-mindedness and integrity (Cao Duan, Ming dynasty; power), diligence and integrity (Kuang Zhong, Ming; performance of duty), loyalty and integrity (Zhen Dexiu, Southern Song; political allegiance), filial piety and integrity (Huang Tingjian, Northern Song; family ethics) and purity and integrity (Zhou Dunyi, Northern Song; inner cultivation). Each section ends with a present-day problem among Party members and cadres.

Sun presents each pair as mutually dependent. Public spirit is the basis of integrity, and integrity gives public spirit substance. Diligence secures integrity, and integrity directs diligence. Loyalty and integrity imply each other, though Sun notes that Zhen's loyalty was owed to the feudal monarch. Filial piety is the emotional root of integrity. Inner purity is needed for integrity, which in turn makes purity concrete. Sun links these to current failings: obstructive red tape, passivity, double-dealing, nepotism and family-based corruption, and cadres who refrain from corruption only under pressure.

Sun concludes that Party members should unite public spirit with integrity, combine diligence with honesty, join absolute loyalty with self-discipline, run clean households, and move from "not daring" and "not being able" to corrupt to "not wanting" to. The article calls for passing on these "integrity genes" and strengthening conscious commitment to clean governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars use classical Chinese ethics to frame contemporary anti-corruption education.
quoteEn: Strengthening a culture of integrity in the new era depends not only on high-pressure deterrence and the cage of institutions, but even more on the moral self-awareness of Party members and cadres, who should keep rising from "not daring" and "not being able" to the state of "not wanting".
quoteZh: 加强新时代廉洁文化建设，既要靠高压震慑和制度笼子，更要靠党员干部内心的道德自觉，从“不敢”“不能”向“不想”的境界不断升华。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Party anti-corruption work for values, norms and education that promote honesty and probity among officials and society.
Party members who hold official or leadership posts, the main audience of Party discipline and integrity education.

t: The "five organs", "six viscera", "four beams" and "eight pillars": focal points for building an autonomous knowledge system of Chinese discipline inspection and supervision studies
zh: “五脏”“六腑”“四梁”“八柱”：构建中国纪检监察学自主知识体系的着力点
source: Administration and Law (Xingzheng yu Fa), 2025 no. 11
paras: After discipline inspection and supervision studies became a first-level discipline in September 2022, building its autonomous knowledge system became a shared task for the field. Sun Dawei asks where the effort should concentrate. The article argues that existing studies treat only the discipline system and pick scattered points, and proposes a three-dimensional framework. It links the "five organs" and "six viscera" to the disciplinary system, the "four beams" to the academic system and the "eight pillars" to the discourse system.

The article first reviews work by Wang Xu, Chen Yafei, Guo Weilu, Zhang Zhen, Jiang Laiyong and Xu Yuzhen, and finds it fragmented. It then draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on an autonomous knowledge system, which the author reads as comprising disciplinary, academic and discourse systems. Three sections follow, each defining its metaphor, assessing current progress and naming a priority for the future.

The metaphors are borrowed from sociologists. Fei Xiaotong's "five organs" are five kinds of institution: learned societies, research institutes, departments, libraries and documentation centres, and publishing houses. His "six viscera" are six core courses. Chen Guangjin's "four beams" are theoretical, historical, methodological and applied knowledge. The "eight pillars" are the distinctive concepts, judgments, propositions and categories, together with the representative works, scholars, schools and doctrines. Sun reports that the organs have grown quickly, citing the China Discipline Inspection and Supervision Association, new institutes at universities, the publisher China Fangzheng Press and new journals. The viscera lag because courses are poorly designed and theoretical talent is scarce. Applied, historical and methodological knowledge have advanced through practice, integrity-culture work and survey research. Theory remains the weakest beam, still shaped by Western frameworks such as principal–agent theory. In the discourse system, annual anti-corruption buzzwords remain political language that has not yet been turned into academic concepts.

Sun concludes that the priorities are to strengthen the six viscera, to develop theory with Chinese characteristics, and to turn political discourse into systematic academic concepts. These steps, Sun argues, would make the system more systematic, original and fit for its time, and would support international communication of Chinese anti-corruption discourse. Sun ties the task to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese legal and Party-discipline scholar sets out an agenda for building a new discipline, or if you follow the institutional growth of anti-corruption scholarship in China.
quoteEn: However, these anti-corruption buzzwords are in essence still political discourse, and for them to become truly distinctive concepts, political discourse must be converted into academic discourse.
quoteZh: 但是，这些反腐热词本质上还是一种政治话语，而要从反腐热词真正成为标识性概念就需要将政治话语转化为学术话语

glossary.explanation: A first-level academic discipline formally established in China in 2022. It studies the work of Party discipline inspection commissions and state supervisory commissions.
A phrase used in Xi Jinping's speeches for a Chinese-originated body of social science knowledge, made up of disciplinary, academic and discourse systems.
The official name for China's development path under the Party's leadership, promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

t: Grasping the scientific content and practical requirements of the anti-corruption path with Chinese characteristics
zh: 深刻把握中国特色反腐败之路的科学内涵与实践要求
paras: This commentary, published in the People's Daily in March 2026, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party has found an anti-corruption path with Chinese characteristics. That path, Xi said, operates under the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee and treats symptoms and root causes together while advancing the three "not" goals as one whole. Li Li argues that this formulation is both a summary of experience and a theoretical advance, and that grasping it matters for what the article calls a protracted battle against corruption.

The article has three parts. The first presents centralised and unified Party leadership as the fundamental precondition and political advantage of the path. The second treats the integrated push for "not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt" as the methodology of addressing symptoms and root causes together. The third sets out the path's internal logic and what Li calls its comparative advantages, in governance method, in popular standing and in "embedded governance".

In Li's account, centralised leadership allows strategic deployment beyond local and short-term considerations, breaks departmental barriers and entrenched interests, and turns institutional strengths into anti-corruption capacity. The three "nots" are described as mutually dependent: relentless punishment creates deterrence, supervision and institutional reform (including reform of the national supervisory system) build constraints on power, and ideological education and a culture of integrity create inner commitment. On the comparative side, Li contends that some countries rely on checks within the administration or on public opinion and electoral pressure, which the author says leads to departmental shielding, fragmentation and short-term results. By contrast, Li says the Chinese path draws on strategic coordination, organisational mobilisation under democratic centralism and the Party's own drive for self-purification.

Li further argues that the path rests on a people-centred standard, with mass and media supervision channelled through institutions and public satisfaction used to judge results. Anti-corruption is said to be embedded in national governance, so that cases drive reform, supervision covers all public officials and a cleaner political environment supports Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official People's Daily line presents China's anti-corruption model and its claimed advantages over other countries' approaches.
quoteEn: The anti-corruption struggle is highly complex and arduous; only by upholding and strengthening the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee can it go beyond local and short-term considerations and achieve overall, systematic strategic deployment and integration of forces.
quoteZh: 反腐败斗争具有高度复杂性与艰巨性，只有坚持和加强党中央集中统一领导，才能超越局部和短期考量，进行全局性、系统性的战略部署与力量整合。

t: Why strict supervision and enforcement of discipline is a sharp tool of the Party's self-reform
zh: 从严监督执纪为什么是党的自我革命的利器
paras: This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the 21st collective study session of the Political Bureau that strict supervision and enforcement of discipline is a "sharp tool" of the Party's self-reform. The piece, written by Cai Jue for a university research centre on the Party's innovative theory, argues that supervision and discipline are what keep the fight against corruption from becoming a formality. In its account, they are essential to ensuring that the Party never degenerates in character.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why strict supervision and discipline matter, the second identifies their core requirements, and the third proposes practical paths. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and on the record of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

In the first part, the author gives three reasons. Strict discipline is said to be needed to preserve the Party's vanguard character and purity. It is also described as the key to winning popular trust, and as a guarantee of long-term governance and Chinese modernization. The second part sets three requirements: strictness across the board and to the end, catching problems early and keeping supervision regular and lasting, and strict enforcement with every violation investigated. The author treats the "four forms" of supervision and discipline as the means of applying this. The third part is the most practical. It calls for tackling Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline together, with ideological education, the Central Committee's eight-point regulations and regular discipline education. It also calls for linking the Party's internal supervision with external forms such as people's congresses, audit and public opinion, with special focus on the "key minority" of leading cadres. It further proposes investigating and handling misconduct and corruption together, since the author treats them as sharing one root. Finally, it asks for a disciplined inspection and supervision force that is itself subject to the strictest constraint.

Cai concludes that the depth of the Party's self-reform depends directly on how effective strict supervision and discipline are. The author calls for keeping up this strictness, presented as a permanent task, against complacency and against any expectation that the campaign will ease. The text is a Party-theory commentary rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register account of how current Party discourse links discipline, supervision and anti-corruption to the idea of self-reform.
quoteEn: Strict supervision and enforcement of discipline is the key to ensuring that the Party's self-reform advances effectively and achieves real results, and it must be pursued consistently and without relaxation.
quoteZh: 从严监督执纪是确保党的自我革命有效推进和取得实效的关键所在，必须一以贯之、毫不松懈地抓下去。

glossary.explanation: A phrase Xi Jinping has stressed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It means the Party's continuous self-cleansing and correction, presented as its second answer to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and decline.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the campaign to tighten Party discipline, combat corruption and improve Party conduct that began after 2012.

t: Ancient Chinese supervision systems: evolution, characteristics and lessons
zh: 中国古代监察制度：演变、特征及启示
source: Journal of China Executive Leadership Academy Jinggangshan, 2025 no. 6
paras: Qu Xiaoshuang asks what the long history of supervision (jiancha) institutions in ancient China can teach contemporary China. The article argues that these institutions, which arose early and were tightly designed, served to protect imperial power and discipline officialdom. In Qu's reading, they remained dependent on the monarch and so could never effectively restrain supreme power, while offering experience that is relevant to deepening supervision reform today.

The article first defines supervision power as a power parallel to legislative, executive and judicial power. It then traces five periods: the Pre-Qin beginnings, formation under the Qin and Han, maturity under the Sui and Tang, transformation under the Song, and full elaboration under the Ming and Qing. It also discusses debates over when the system originated. Qu singles out the Han, Tang and Ming as the most typical stages.

Qu draws out three threads. First, supervision officials sent to the localities repeatedly acquired military and administrative power, as with Han regional inspectors, Tang military governors and Ming–Qing governors-general and governors. The author argues that this produced separatism and corrupt officialdom and reflected a flaw in one-directional, top-down supervision. Second, the inspection tour (xunshi) system developed from temporary dispatches to standing, professionalised practice, and Qu compares it with the Party's present system. Third, supervisory officials were selected, promoted, rotated and punished under strict rules, with high rank and rewards to motivate them.

Qu concludes that ancient supervision, rooted in imperial power and an integrated power structure, lacked internal checks and could be turned into a weapon of factional struggle. Qu contrasts this with the Party's full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the 2018 Supervision Law and the Party's self-reform. The article calls for strengthening Party leadership of discipline inspection and supervision, building a Party-regulation system, and developing discipline inspection and supervision studies as a discipline that draws on ancient experience. Read the original if you study the history of Chinese supervision institutions or how Party scholars draw on imperial-era practice to frame current anti-corruption reform.
quoteEn: Ancient China's supervision system took centralisation as its aim, treating supervisory power as the power over governing power and supervisory officials as the officials who govern officials, and it explored both the independence of the supervisory system and the specialisation of its officials.

t: Digital discipline inspection and supervision: using technology to strengthen the penetrating power of anti-corruption work
zh: 数字纪检监察：以科技赋能提高反腐败穿透力
paras: Shi Pengpeng, a deputy dean and professor at the School of Discipline Inspection and Supervision of China University of Political Science and Law, takes up a call from Xi Jinping at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) to keep raising the "penetrating power" of anti-corruption work. In this commentary for Guangming Daily, Shi argues that digital discipline inspection and supervision, built on big data, artificial intelligence and information platforms, is the necessary means. Technology, in this account, shifts supervision from reliance on human experience and after-the-fact investigation to embedding oversight in the whole process of power's operation.

The piece has three parts. The first sets out why technology matters for anti-corruption work at present. The second explains what penetrating power means and what it requires. The third proposes four practical paths. Shi places the argument within full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Chinese modernization and the modernization of the national governance system.

Shi's core claim is that penetrating power means looking through the surface of power's operation to its allocation structure, operating mechanisms and institutional risks, not merely finding case leads. Three requirements follow: penetrating structure, through methods such as power maps and process modelling that expose blind spots and overlapping functions; penetrating process, through real-time monitoring that moves risk warning forward; and penetrating the mechanisms by which corruption arises, by mining past case data to build risk models and indicators. The four paths are integrating data into a single network, using correlation analysis to turn hidden risks into signals, merging technology with the handling of leads, inspection and investigation, and building institutions so that technology works in a standardised, law-based way.

Shi concludes that converting technological advantages into institutional advantages, and data into governance effectiveness, will consolidate the results of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. It would also help sustain the "tough, protracted and overall" fight against corruption. The author presents technology as part of the institutional basis of the Party's self-supervision, not as a mere efficiency tool. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale for digital supervision in China's anti-corruption system, and of how its proponents describe the link between data analysis and institutional reform.

t: Using rigorous institutions and rigid enforcement to lock power in an institutional cage
zh: 以严密制度和刚性执行把权力关进制度笼子
paras: This newspaper commentary in Guangming Daily (9 February 2026) takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection that the Party's self-reform centres on governing power. Song argues that locking power in an institutional cage is an important task of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and that it requires rigorous institutions together with rigid enforcement.

The piece has three parts. The first explains why governing power is the key to the Party's self-reform. The second sets out three levels of institutional governance of power: supply, enforcement and authority. The third turns to how the cage is made to work in practice.

Song argues that power is a double-edged sword, and that for a long-governing Marxist party the main risk is power operating without rules. Drawing on the eight-point regulation introduced after the 18th Party Congress (2012), the author says that clear institutional boundaries changed the political climate. On institutions, Song reads Xi's formula of rules that are "dense but not cumbersome" as a call for coverage that is comprehensive and effective. Enforcement must be rigid, so that violations carry a cost. Authority depends on whether rules bind the most powerful, which Song treats as a political principle and not a technical matter.

For implementation, Song calls for top leaders to set an example, for education that leads officials to know the rules and stand in awe of them, and for greater openness in Party and government affairs so that power operates in the sunlight. Song presents these as a chain running from leadership responsibility through understanding to the operating environment, and ties it to securing the goals of the 15th Five-Year Plan period. t: Multiple dimensions of building a culture of integrity in the new era
zh: 新时代廉洁文化建设的多维向度
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 27 January 2026
paras: This short commentary asks how a culture of integrity (lianjie wenhua) should be built in the new era, taking its cue from Xi Jinping's call to strengthen it. Bai defines it as a continuing undertaking that uses ideological education, institutional norms and cultural dissemination to create a social atmosphere that honours probity and builds a cultural ecosystem. The article argues that this requires work on four fronts at once: ideas, institutions, technology and society.

The piece is organised under four headings. The first covers the spiritual and ideological foundations. The second covers a network for supervising the exercise of power. The third covers a technology system for "smart" anti-corruption work. The fourth covers cultivating a social ecology that honours integrity. Each section lists three or so concrete measures.

On the ideological side, Bai says Marxist theory on the nature of power and the people's principal position is the theoretical source of integrity culture, and that Party history and Party-spirit education bases should convey the Party's fine traditions. On institutions, Bai points to Party regulations issued since the 18th Party Congress (2012), checks and balances among decision-making, executive and supervisory powers, a multi-level supervision system and strict accountability. On technology, Bai proposes an integrity big-data platform that monitors funds, approvals and procurement, AI risk-prediction models and case-clue screening, and blockchain to record power-related data immutably. On society, Bai calls for wider channels for public reporting, regular integrity education that extends to off-duty hours and family conduct, and use of both positive role models and negative cases.

Bai concludes that integrity culture is a systemic project needing participation from the whole of society, so that it becomes custom and common practice. The article gives a concise checklist of policy directions in line with the Central Committee General Office's opinions on strengthening integrity culture. t: Advancing the anti-corruption struggle with greater clarity and resolve
zh: 更加清醒坚定地推进反腐败斗争
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 4 February 2026, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (January 2026) to advance the anti-corruption struggle "with greater clarity and resolve". Wang Dongqi argues that the situation remains severe and complex, and that the Party must keep up a high-pressure posture and push forward the Party's self-reform.

The piece has three parts. The first assesses the current situation, citing 2025 case statistics. The second describes new trends in corruption and how to sharpen the ability to see through them. The third sets out how to advance, in an integrated way, the aims of making officials unafraid, unable and unwilling to be corrupt.

Wang argues that although the anti-corruption struggle has achieved what is described as an overwhelming victory, the "two remainings" persist: the situation is still severe and complex, and rooting out the soil of corruption is still arduous. The article cites 2025 figures, including 65 centrally managed cadres investigated and 261,788 people given Party or administrative sanctions for breaches of the eight-point regulation. It notes that corruption is becoming more hidden: networked rather than linear structures, intermediaries and proxies, and use of blockchain and virtual currency. Wang proposes "seeing through" layered structures and disguises to the real beneficiaries and building a digital discipline-inspection and supervision system with big-data platforms. The three "nots" are treated as one organic whole rather than three stages: fear of punishment is the premise, institutional constraint the key, and ideological conviction the foundation.

To implement this, Wang calls for clearer responsibility systems, with first-responsibility on Party "top leaders"; for rules that align the granting, use and restraint of power and make it transparent and traceable; and for supervision reform that links Party supervision with people's and other forms of oversight. The author also stresses self-discipline alongside external discipline and integrity culture. t: Caging power in the system more scientifically and effectively
zh: 更加科学有效地把权力关进制度笼子
paras: This commentary in Guangming Daily responds to Xi Jinping's remarks at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (2026). Xi said that the Party's self-reform centres on governing power, and that caging power in the system is an important task of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. He Husheng argues that this requires strengthening institutional control over power, rule-based use of authority, and better mechanisms of restraint and oversight, so that power serves the people's fundamental interests.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the core meaning of the policy; the second names problems to address during the 15th Five-Year Plan period; the third proposes ways to apply systematic remedies. It relies heavily on Xi's formulations, quoting him on power, institutions, sunlight and anti-corruption.

In the first part, He treats power as a double-edged sword whose purpose is to benefit the people. He links the cage to three points: the people as the source of power, systematic integration of restraint and oversight, and deepening the Party's self-reform so that it leads a "great social revolution". On problems, He names three pairs of risks. One is institutions that are loosely designed or weakly enforced (a "cattle pen for cats", a "paper cage for tigers"), with new forms of hidden corruption in emerging sectors. Another is the need to balance the "key minority" of leaders with the "vast majority" of officials. The last is the contrast between impatience for quick results and complacency in the anti-corruption struggle. He says that corruption stock has not been cleared in some power- and resource-heavy areas and that old problems could rebound.

He proposes three measures: unite rule-making with discipline enforcement, with "zero tolerance" for undermining rules; combine leadership by example with discipline education so that officials revere power and the law; and let power operate in the sunlight. The last includes digital platforms embedding risk controls and a Party-led supervision system linking discipline, supervisory, inspection and other forms of oversight. He concludes that these steps would support Chinese modernization. t: Strict supervision with force, caring encouragement with warmth
st: Cultivating young cadres should rely on "grasping with both hands"
zh: 严管约束有力度 厚爱激励有温度

paras: This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 16 January 2026, asks how the Party should cultivate young cadres. Liu Lianjun argues that it must "grasp with both hands": strict management and caring support, incentives and constraints, with both hands firm.

Liu opens with Xi Jinping's remarks on reliable successors and with the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, which called for targeting corruption among the "key few" and young cadres. The piece then describes young cadres' strengths and weaknesses, recalls the Party's past cultivation work from Mao Zedong to the post-2012 period, and ends with concrete measures.

In Liu's account, young cadres are innovative and energetic but, being inexperienced, may yield to temptation or lose motivation after setbacks. Liu holds that strictness without warmth harms their drive and resilience, while kindness without strictness weakens their political ability and sense of responsibility. Strictness means ideological education, instruction in Party discipline and law, and clear rules. Warmth means a merit-based promotion system, careful application of the "three distinctions" to errors, prompt clarification of false accusations, and political, ideological, daily-life and psychological care.

Liu concludes that only a combination of the two approaches can sustain young cadres through what the article calls a marathon rather than a sprint, and produce cadres who are loyal, responsible and clean. t: Using a systems perspective to link improving conduct, enforcing discipline and fighting corruption
zh: 以系统观念推动正风肃纪反腐相贯通
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 21 October 2025
paras: Liu and Wu take up the Party's formula of 'integrating' work on conduct, discipline and anti-corruption (zhengfeng, suji, fanfu). They argue that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee has applied a systems perspective to Party building, and that this perspective should now guide efforts to deepen full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in support of Chinese modernization.

This short commentary is organised in three parts: the underlying rationale for integrating the three tasks, the core meaning of the formula, and practical paths for putting it into effect. The rationale is drawn from Marxist method, the Party's historical experience and current conditions.

On rationale, the authors hold that problems of conduct and corruption are two sides of one coin and share a root, while lax discipline causes both. They trace the practice from the revolutionary period through the campaign against Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan to the post-1978 period. On core meaning, they identify three focal points: wholeness, coordination and dynamism. In their account, improving conduct leads, enforcing discipline guarantees, and fighting corruption clears obstacles, together forming a closed-loop system.

For practice, the authors call for integrated responsibility, with Party committees, discipline commissions, functional departments and individual cadres each fulfilling defined duties. They also call for integrated institutions, which would fix effective experience in rules, close loopholes behind the interweaving of misconduct and corruption, and apply Party discipline and state law together. t: Building a comprehensive, multi-level system for cultivating a culture of integrity
zh: 构建全方位多层次的廉洁文化培育体系
paras: This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 16 October 2025, asks how a culture of integrity (lianjie wenhua) can be built into a lasting system rather than a one-off campaign. Zhang Xianfeng argues that it is a systemic undertaking that cannot be completed in a day or by a single actor. It needs a cultivation system that is comprehensive in coverage, multi-level in penetration and wide in reach.

Zhang begins from the policy background: the Party's emphasis since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the 2022 General Office guideline on integrity culture in the new era, and the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, which called for a three-year action plan for 2025–2027. The article is then organised under three headings: differentiated guidance, faster innovation in methods, and integrated promotion.

On differentiated guidance, Zhang sets out distinct approaches for four groups. Leading cadres are the 'key minority' and need mandatory, cautionary education, risk-point screening and the 'cage of institutions' to constrain power. Ordinary Party members need discipline awareness and public integrity pledges. Students need integrated primary-to-university education, and the general public needs cultural products and easy reporting channels with protection for whistle-blowers. On innovation, Zhang proposes digital tools such as a 'smart integrity education' cloud platform, big-data risk early warning and virtual-reality exhibition halls. Zhang also proposes integrity-themed cultural brands, cartoon figures and creative merchandise, and the placing of integrity elements in everyday settings such as parks, festivals and village life.

On integrated promotion, Zhang calls for a closed-loop management system with a joint conference mechanism, task lists broken down to individuals, and inclusion of results in the Party conduct and ideological work responsibility assessments. Zhang also proposes a shared resource platform with personalised content recommendation, and an evaluation mechanism using quantified indicators and independent third-party assessors. Feedback would then drive a plan–execute–check–adjust cycle, moving integrity culture from 'visible coverage' to 'effective coverage'. t: The internal logic of Xi Jinping's important discourse on discipline inspection and supervision work
zh: 习近平关于纪检监察工作重要论述的内在逻辑
source: Research on National Modernization Construction (国家现代化建设研究), 2025 no. 2
paras: Shi Wei and He Youying ask what logic runs through Xi Jinping's statements on the work of the Party's discipline inspection and supervision organs. They argue that these statements form the "discipline inspection and supervision chapter" of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and are held together by a consistent line of materialist dialectics. The central task they identify is advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through Chinese modernization.

The article is organised around four pairs of dialectical unities, each tied to one aspect of the work: goals and problems (objectives and tasks), overall synergy and key priorities (direction and content), self-supervision and supervision by the people (principles and attitude), and strict management and loving care (building the supervisory force). The authors draw on Xi's speeches at plenary sessions of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and on earlier remarks about "who supervises the discipline commissions".

In the first move, the authors read Xi's goal orientation as keeping the organs focused on upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee and centralised, unified leadership. His problem orientation rests on the "four tests", the "four dangers" and the "problems unique to a large party", and the authors present it as a matter of identifying principal contradictions. Second, they say a systemic view calls for coordinating Party, supervisory, inspection and other forms of supervision and for "jointly investigating and addressing" misconduct and corruption. A focus on key points means watching "top leaders" and key issues, including sectors with concentrated power and funds and the "micro-corruption" that affects farmers. Third, they contend that because supervisors must themselves be supervised, the organs must show "thoroughly self-reforming" spirit, in a force that is "strict yet caring".

The authors conclude that the discourse shows the wisdom of materialist dialectics and gives theoretical guidance and a guide to action for the organs. They add that it should help cadres strengthen their dialectical thinking and their ability to handle complex situations. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how current Party theory frames the logic of anti-corruption and supervision work, and which Xi texts it draws on.
quoteEn: The distinctive nature of the discipline inspection and supervision organs' political responsibility and mission lies in their dedicated supervisory role; so in exercising supervisory power they must not supervise only others and not themselves, and must uphold the dialectical unity of self-supervision and supervision by the people.

t: Consciously guiding all discipline inspection and supervision work with Xi Jinping's important thinking on the Party's self-reform
zh: 自觉用习近平总书记关于党的自我革命的重要思想统领纪检监察一切工作
paras: This commentary, published in Study Times on 12 January 2024, responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI). Gong Tanghua, who heads the CCDI's supervision team at the State Council's SASAC, argues that discipline inspection and supervision bodies must bring their thinking and action into line with the speech. In the article's account, they must treat Xi's important thinking on the Party's self-reform as the guide for all their work.

The article has three parts. The first interprets the content and significance of the thinking, which Gong calls the plenum's most important political outcome. The second turns to the strategy for a decisive and protracted anti-corruption struggle, and applies it to central state-owned enterprises. The third sets out requirements for building up discipline inspection and supervision cadres themselves.

Gong presents the thinking as powerful in three ways: in the truth of its theory, in its practical guidance and in its spiritual appeal. It answers why, how and by what means the Party can reform itself, and forms the self-reform chapter of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. For SASAC and the central enterprises, Gong would advance the “three no's” together: not daring to be corrupt, not being able to and not wanting to. Under the first, the article names key sectors (finance, energy, pharmaceuticals, infrastructure) and key links (mergers, personnel decisions, procurement, bidding, overseas investment). Under the second, it calls for institutional reform, case analysis and supervision of top leaders. Under the third, it proposes disciplinary education, warning-education bases and a rejection of the idea that central enterprises are special.

Gong concludes that discipline inspection personnel must turn the blade inward and be models of self-reform. He asks them to lead in theoretical study, political loyalty, struggle and personal integrity, and to resist what the article calls corrupt Western values. He also proposes measures on selecting and rotating cadres and on talent pools. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party discipline official applies the Party's self-reform doctrine to the state-owned asset sector and to the supervisors themselves.
quoteEn: As the specialised organs of intra-Party supervision and state supervision, and as the sword with which the Party and people defend state power and safeguard national rejuvenation, discipline inspection and supervision bodies bear special political responsibility and a glorious mission, and must themselves be thoroughly steeled.
quoteZh: 纪检监察机关作为党内监督、国家监察专责机关，作为党和人民维护国家政权、捍卫民族复兴的利剑，肩负特殊政治责任和光荣使命任务，自身必须十分过硬。

Refers to the Party's discipline inspection commissions and the state supervisory commissions. Since 2018 they have worked together, often through shared personnel.

t: The theoretical content and contemporary value of Mao Zedong's thought on Party discipline building
zh: 毛泽东关于党的纪律建设思想的理论内涵及时代价值
authors: Party Committee of the China Academy of Discipline Inspection and Supervision
source: China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News, 28 December 2023, p. 8
paras: This article, a collective piece by the Party Committee of the China Academy of Discipline Inspection and Supervision, asks what Mao Zedong's thinking on Party discipline contains and what it offers the Party today. It argues that Mao applied Marxist principles to Chinese conditions and built a body of thought whose constant themes were strengthening Party leadership, enforcing political discipline and stressing ideological education. In the authors' view, this thought remains relevant to strengthening discipline in the new era.

The article has three parts. The first traces the origins of Mao's thought: the proletarian party's nature and original mission, the adaptation of Marxist party-building theory to China, and practical needs in revolution and construction. The second sets out five elements of its content: the status of discipline, its core requirements, ideological education, institutions and rules, and enforcement. The third draws lessons for the present.

On the authors' account, Mao defined discipline as the "guarantee for carrying out the line" and made the "four subordinations" (individual to organisation, minority to majority, lower level to higher level, the whole Party to the Central Committee) the most important discipline. The article treats ideological education as the "first-class task" for cultivating "conscious discipline", and cites Mao's insistence that discipline be codified in rules such as reporting systems and the Party committee system. It also presents the principle of "punishing past errors to prevent future ones and curing the sickness to save the patient" as pairing strictness with care, citing Mao's stress that Communists must meet a stricter standard than ordinary citizens.

For the present, the authors call for guiding discipline building with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, centring on political discipline, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. They also call for treating Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline together, integrating discipline building into the wider system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and advancing the "three no-corruptions" (not daring, not being able, not wanting to be corrupt) as one whole. Read the original if you want an official Party-institutional account of how Mao's discipline thinking is linked to current anti-corruption and Party-building doctrine.

t: Studying and implementing Xi Jinping's strategic thought on the Party's self-reform and building up discipline inspection cadres themselves
zh: 学习贯彻习近平总书记关于党的自我革命战略思想 扎实推进纪检干部队伍自身建设
paras: Writing in 2023, Liao Wenhui presents a study-and-implementation commentary on what the author calls Xi Jinping's strategic thought on the Party's self-reform. Liao argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi has set out this thought as an original contribution to the Marxist theory of party building. In Liao's account it also deepens understanding of how to build a Marxist party that stays in power for the long term. The article then applies the thought to the ongoing education and rectification of discipline inspection and supervision cadres.

The text has two parts. The first sets out the content of the thought: Xi's statements from 2016 to the 20th Party Congress (2022), why self-reform is needed, and how it has been carried out. The second turns to the discipline inspection cadre corps itself and lists four requirements: political tempering, theoretical armament, a fighting spirit, and strict self-discipline.

On why self-reform is needed, Liao points to problems the 20th Party Congress report attributed to the period before 2012, including weakened Party leadership, formalism, bureaucratism and corruption. Liao adds that the Party's "four tests" and "four dangers" will persist, so full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is "always on the road". Liao presents self-reform as the Party's defining trait. It rests on the Party's nature and purpose, which Liao says include having no special interests of its own. On method, Liao lists eight measures, among them political building, centralised education, the eight-point regulations, discipline, inspection tours, Party regulations and an anti-corruption campaign that targets "tigers", "flies" and "foxes".

Liao concludes that discipline inspection bodies are political organs and must hold themselves to higher standards than the cadres they supervise. Liao calls on them to carry out self-examination, guard against the "darkness under the lamp", and become a more disciplined "iron army". They are also to uphold the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a clear example of how the Party's official discourse links self-reform theory to the internal discipline of its own inspection apparatus.
quoteEn: Discipline inspection cadres, as the Party's \"disciplinary force\", do supervisory work that makes enemies. They must hold to their responsibilities and fight everything that undermines Party unity or damages its advanced and pure character, and daring and skill in struggle are extremely important qualities.
quoteZh: 纪检干部作为党的“纪律部队”，干的是监督的活、得罪人的活，要坚守责任担当，同一切破坏党的团结统一、损害党的先进纯洁的人和事作斗争，敢于斗争、善于斗争是极其重要的品格。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping has developed since 2016. It holds that the Communist Party corrects itself through its own efforts, and it is presented as the Party's answer to the problem of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and decline.

t: Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's strategic thinking on the Party's self-reform and building up discipline inspection cadres
zh: 学习贯彻习近平总书记关于党的自我革命战略思想 扎实推进纪检干部队伍自身建设
paras: Liao Wenhui, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in mid-2023, sets out to explain Xi Jinping's strategic thinking on the Party's self-reform and to draw out what it requires of the Party's own discipline inspection cadres. The article presents the thinking as an original contribution to the Marxist doctrine of party building and as an important part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It argues that it deepens understanding of how to build a Marxist party that governs for the long term.

The piece has two parts. The first reviews the thinking itself, tracing Xi's statements from 2016 through the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It then asks why the Party needs self-reform and how it has been carried out. The second part turns to the campaign of education and rectification among discipline inspection and supervision cadres, launched in 2023, and sets four requirements for them.

Liao gives two reasons for self-reform. Before the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article says, the Party faced serious problems: weak Party leadership, wavering convictions, formalism, bureaucracy, privilege and corruption. The Party also still faces what it calls the four tests and four dangers, together with the problems peculiar to a large party, so self-reform must be permanent. Liao presents the Party's nature and mission as the source of its willingness to correct itself, since it claims no special interests of its own. Eight measures are listed: political building, centralised education, organisational rectification, the eight-point decision on conduct, discipline, supervision, rule-based governance and anti-corruption work.

Liao concludes that discipline inspection cadres must meet a higher standard, because their organs are political organs. They should show absolute loyalty to the Party Central Committee, with Xi at its core, and build their convictions through theoretical study. They should also develop a fighting spirit and the skills to go with it, and hold themselves to strict personal standards. These include self-examination and guarding against the problem of those who police others failing to look at themselves. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal official frames self-reform and the tasks assigned to discipline inspection cadres in the 2023 rectification campaign.
quoteEn: The greatness of the Communist Party of China lies not in never making mistakes, but in never shying away from its ailments, daring to face problems squarely, and relying on its own strength to correct errors and solve problems.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的伟大不在于不犯错误，而在于从不讳疾忌医，敢于直面问题，依靠自身力量纠正错误、解决问题。

glossary.explanation: A concept developed under Xi Jinping since 2016. It describes the Party's capacity to correct its own errors and purge its own ranks, and is presented as the answer to the historical cycle of rise and decline.

t: The establishment and initial operation of the administrative supervision system in New China (1949–1954)
zh: 新中国行政监察体制的建立与初步运行（1949—1954年）
source: Contemporary China History Studies (Dangdai Zhongguoshi Yanjiu), 2023 no. 1
paras: Xu Xing asks how New China's administrative supervision system was built and how it worked in its first five years, a stretch that earlier scholarship has covered thinly. Existing work, the author notes, concentrates on intra-Party supervision or on today's national supervision reform. Xu argues that the 1949–1954 system, created under Party leadership and shaped above all by Zhou Enlai, played a real historical role in fighting corruption and bureaucratism and still offers lessons for current reform.

The article opens with the roots of the system in the revolutionary base areas: the Soviet-period Workers' and Peasants' Inspection departments, the border-region assemblies of the anti-Japanese war, and the North China People's Supervisory Court of 1948. It then describes the founding of the People's Supervisory Commission under the Government Administration Council, its 1950 trial organizational regulations and its internal departments. Next it covers how the commission operated, including the national supervision conferences of 1951 and 1953, and assesses its results. A closing section draws four implications for the present.

Xu identifies three main achievements. The commission focused on financial and economic management, investigating accidents such as the Yiluo coal mine gas explosion; it joined the Three-Antis campaign, disciplining thousands of cadres and helping to handle the Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan case; and it built a five-level network that, by September 1954, reached nearly 4,000 organs with close to 20,000 supervisory cadres. The author highlights working principles such as combining top-down inspection with bottom-up supervision by the masses, and combining punishment with education. Xu also reports the dual leadership structure, the abolition of the large administrative regions in 1954, and the replacement of the commission by a Ministry of Supervision.

Xu concludes that Zhou Enlai's supervisory thinking supports clean government, mass participation, rigorous management of supervisory cadres and Party leadership. The article links the 1950s move from separate Party and state supervision bodies to later reform, ending with the 2018 National Supervisory Commission and the Supervision Law. Xu presents this as evidence that merging Party and state supervision strengthens constraints on power. Read the original if you want a detailed institutional history of early People's Republic supervision, with figures, regulations and case examples, written from an official Party-history perspective.
quoteEn: Zhou Enlai's thinking on administrative supervision and his initial practice advanced the sinicization of Marxist supervision theory.
quoteZh: 周恩来的行政监察思想及初步实践促进了马克思主义监察理论中国化的发展。

glossary.explanation: A mass campaign launched in late 1951 against corruption, waste and bureaucratism among Party and state personnel. It was accompanied by public trials and severe punishments in prominent cases.

glossary.explanation: The central administrative supervision body of 1949–1954, set up under the Government Administration Council. It oversaw state organs and officials and handled public complaints, until replaced by the Ministry of Supervision in 1954.

t: Clean-government building in the Chinese Soviet Republic and its valuable experience
zh: 中华苏维埃共和国廉政建设及其宝贵经验
paras: Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), which restated that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform are "always on the road", Chen Shifa looks back to the Chinese Soviet Republic (founded at Ruijin, Jiangxi, in the early 1930s). The commentary argues that this republic was a pioneering attempt at a new type of state power, a prototype of the later People's Republic and a testing ground for Party governance. In Chen's view, it was also an important early stage of the Party leading social revolution through its own self-reform, with clean government as its core content.

The piece is a short newspaper article organised around four contributions of the Soviet period: building a broadly democratic new regime, creating an unprecedentedly clean government, constructing a comprehensive supervision mechanism, and spreading a culture of integrity in the service of the people. It draws on the Constitutional Outline of the Chinese Soviet Republic, election regulations, anti-corruption decrees and statements by Mao Zedong, Zhang Wentian and Xiang Ying, together with descriptive detail about the government's offices and staffing.

Chen's central claim is that clean government rested on institutional design and not only on personal virtue. Democracy is said to have been made real through mass election campaigns, small electoral districts, universal suffrage for the exploited, and rights of supervision, dismissal, re-election and recall over deputies. The government is portrayed as lean and close to the masses: thirteen bodies housed in an ancestral hall, unpaid officials living on small food allowances, and systems such as the duty-deputy and cadre-labour arrangements. Supervision is described as multi-layered, with Party supervisory committees, a workers' and peasants' inspection department, "light cavalry" teams, press columns exposing misconduct, revolutionary courts, and zero tolerance of both embezzlement and waste.

Chen concludes that the Soviet Republic opened a new chapter in building clean government in Chinese history, and that its experience and "red genes" retain strong practical value as a revolutionary lineage the Party must carry forward. The article offers no new archival research but gives a concise official-historical account of how the early Soviet period is now presented in the anti-corruption discourse. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars link the Jiangxi Soviet era to the current campaign for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.
quoteEn: The founding of the Chinese Soviet Republic gave the political ecology a completely fresh look, and it has been described as the \"most clean-handed government in history\".
quoteZh: 中华苏维埃共和国的建立使政治生态气象一新，被喻为“史上空前廉洁的政府”。

t: Rethinking the explanatory models of anti-corruption theory in contemporary China
st: Corruption and anti-corruption as the production and use of domination and anti-domination power
zh: 当代中国廉政理论解释模式的再思考
source: Study and Exploration (Xuexi yu Tansuo), 2022 no. 2
paras: Peng Bin and Zhu Yajiao take up a gap in Chinese research on clean government. Existing studies explain corruption through institutions, rights, morality or class, and all treat abuse of power as its cause. The authors argue that this treats power as nothing but domination. In their view corruption is the conversion of official authority into "power as domination" for private gain, while anti-corruption is the Party and government producing, activating and using "power as anti-domination". They propose this as a new, power-centred account.

The article has three parts. The first summarises four existing explanatory models: "institutional anti-corruption", "rights anti-corruption", "moral anti-corruption" and "class anti-corruption", each with representative Chinese scholars. The second sets out the authors' own perspective, including the case of Lai Xiaomin, former chairman of China Huarong Asset Management, as shown in the documentary series State Supervision. It also covers the anti-corruption system built since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third re-reads each of the four models through anti-domination power.

The central move is to reject the equation of power with domination, which the authors link to Weber and to Lord Acton's dictum on power and corruption. Because actors can mobilise economic, social, cultural and symbolic resources against domination, the authors hold that power can also take an anti-dominating form. They describe an anti-domination power system inside the political system (the eight-point rules, the Supervision Law, the National Supervisory Commission, intra-Party supervision) and outside it (petitions, reporting, media exposure, litigation, inspection tours). The second move reinterprets the four models. Institutions supply channels for anti-domination power. Rights depend on state power to be realised. Moral settings shape tendencies toward domination. Class structure conditions whether such power can arise, and the authors tie common prosperity to this last point.

The authors conclude that the power-centred approach does not oppose the four models but absorbs and complements them. In their account it implies a logic led by Party leadership, secured by institutions and law, supported by citizens' rights and morality, and focused on improving social structure. They claim it can correct misunderstandings of the link between power and corruption and yield a more comprehensive explanatory model. They add that building such a system is a long-term task that is "always on the road". Read the original if you study Chinese anti-corruption and discipline-inspection scholarship and want to see how one theoretical framework tries to integrate its main schools.
quoteEn: In this sense, corruption is the act of corrupt actors alienating their official authority into power as domination in order to seek private gain, while anti-corruption is the Party and government producing, activating or using power as anti-domination to prevent and punish corruption.
quoteZh: 在这种意义上，腐败就是腐败主体将其职权异化为支配性权力以谋取私利的行为，反腐败则是党和政府生产、激活或运用反支配性权力以预防和惩治腐败行为。

glossary.explanation: The authors' term for power that actors use to resist, block or punish domination by others. They contrast it with domination-type power, which they see as the form power takes in corruption.
Power understood as the ability to impose one's will on others. The authors treat it as the form into which corrupt officials convert their public authority.
One of four scholarly models. It explains corruption by gaps in, or breaches of, institutions and rules, and stresses building a sound anti-corruption system and rule of law.

The state anti-corruption and supervision body created in 2018 under the national supervision reform. It supervises all public officials and works closely with the Party's discipline inspection organs.
An official goal of shared wealth for all the people. The article links it to reducing social polarisation, which it presents as a social basis for anti-domination power.

t: What are supervisory commissions being set up for?
zh: 设立监察委员会为的是啥？
paras: Writing in late 2016, Dai Lixing asks what the new supervisory commissions are meant to achieve. The article responds to the Central Committee General Office's scheme, issued on 8 November, to pilot reform of the national supervisory system in Beijing, Shanxi and Zhejiang. Dai argues that the commissions, to be created by people's congresses, amount to a "major political reform affecting the overall situation", and that their purpose is to build an anti-corruption body under the Party's unified leadership.

The commentary is organised around three descriptions of the commission: it is "high in position", "heavy in power" and "forceful". Dai first traces the reform's origins to Xi Jinping's speech at the Sixth Plenary Session of the 18th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (early 2016) and to the communiqué of the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (October 2016), which listed supervisory organs alongside people's congresses and governments. A closing section stresses Party leadership.

Dai's first claim is that administrative supervision will be upgraded to national supervision. Supervisory bodies are now attached to governments and departments and so practise "same-body supervision". Once the commissions are elected by people's congresses and answer to them, Dai argues, they gain independence and authority, and the Party's anti-corruption will is turned into state will. The second claim is that coverage will become comprehensive: current supervision misses people's congress, CPPCC, court and procuratorate staff, village heads and some enterprise and public-institution personnel. Third, Dai says dispersed anti-corruption forces (discipline inspection, administrative supervision, prosecutorial anti-graft units, audit) will be merged. The commissions will gain broader investigative means and share personnel with Party discipline commissions, described as "one set of staff, two nameplates". Dai presents this as different from Western multiparty competition and separation of powers.

Dai concludes that the national supervisory system must embody the Party's absolute leadership and ensure that supervision proceeds within the discipline inspection commissions' framework. The scheme places pilot work under a central leading group and under Party committee secretaries in the pilot areas. Dai suggests the reform will help make officials unwilling, unable and unafraid-to-be-corrupt in a closed loop with congress and judicial oversight. Read the original if you want an early, Party-aligned reading of the 2016 supervision reform pilots and the reasoning offered for them.
quoteEn: It must be stressed that the purpose of reforming the national supervisory system is precisely to establish a national anti-corruption body under the Party's unified leadership.
quoteZh: 需要强调的是，国家监察体制改革的目的，就是要建立党统一领导下的国家反腐败工作机构。

glossary.explanation: New state organs piloted from late 2016 and elected by people's congresses to exercise supervisory power over all public officials. They work jointly with Party discipline inspection commissions.

glossary.en: one set of staff, two nameplates
glossary.literal: joint office work (一套人马、两块牌子)
glossary.explanation: An arrangement in which two institutions share the same personnel and premises. Here it refers to the supervisory commission and the Party discipline inspection commission at the same level.
Oversight carried out by a unit within the organisation being overseen, such as administrative supervision bureaus inside governments. Chinese commentators criticise it as weak.

glossary.pinyin: bù gǎn fǔ, bù néng fǔ, bù xiǎng fǔ
glossary.literal: dare not, cannot, do not want to be corrupt
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the post-2012 anti-corruption campaign describing deterrence, institutional constraint and ideological prevention.
